skill: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm / prioritising haemostasis
stem: A 74-year-old man with a known 6.4 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm arrives with sudden severe back pain and syncope. BP is 74/42 mmHg, pulse 128/min, and bedside ultrasound shows an enlarged abdominal aorta. His abdomen is distended, he remains responsive, and the vascular surgeon is available immediately.
ask: Which management priority offers the best chance of survival?
options: Activate vascular resuscitation and urgent operative control while giving carefully targeted blood products.
Administer several litres of crystalloid to normalise blood pressure before involving the vascular team.
Arrange outpatient CT angiography after haemodynamics stabilise because ultrasound cannot prove rupture.
Begin therapeutic heparin because an aortic thrombus is likely to have embolised distally.
Treat the pain with oral analgesia and observe for spontaneous stabilisation of the aneurysm.
explanations: Correct: presume rupture in this context, activate vascular surgery, major-haemorrhage and anaesthetic support, and move toward endovascular or open repair without avoidable delays. Use carefully titrated resuscitation and blood products according to local protocol; advanced imaging is appropriate only when stable enough.

Large crystalloid loads may worsen bleeding and coagulopathy. Resuscitation should support essential perfusion without postponing haemorrhage control, using blood products and senior-directed targets.
CT angiography can define repair anatomy for patients stable enough for scanning, but transfer to routine outpatient imaging is inappropriate in profound shock and suspected rupture.
Heparin can intensify haemorrhage in a ruptured aneurysm. Distal embolisation does not explain the principal acute haemodynamic presentation or justify anticoagulation now.
Analgesia is supportive but does not stop intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal bleeding. Untreated rupture can cause sudden death even after a transient rise in pressure.
pearl: Known large AAA with sudden back/abdominal pain and shock is ruptured AAA until proven otherwise; rapid haemorrhage control is decisive.
pivot: A haemodynamically stable patient with symptomatic AAA may undergo urgent CT angiography to plan repair while vascular support is mobilised.

steps: Assess ABCs and shock; call vascular surgeon, anaesthesia, operating theatre and major-haemorrhage team immediately.
Establish large-bore access, send urgent crossmatch and give targeted blood products with frequent perfusion review.
Expedite endovascular or open operative treatment; obtain CT only if clinically feasible without dangerous delay.
Review lactate, coagulation, renal function, transfusion needs and postoperative organ perfusion.
management.safety: Avoid routine large-volume crystalloid resuscitation or anticoagulation in suspected ruptured AAA.
management.local: Queensland Health Clinical Prioritisation Criteria for symptomatic and ruptured aortic aneurysm.

skill: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia / new thrombosis
stem: A 62-year-old underwent knee replacement eight days ago and has received prophylactic unfractionated heparin. Platelets fall from 245 to 95 × 10^9/L, and ultrasound now confirms a new femoral DVT. She has no active bleeding; the surgical team proposes switching heparin to enoxaparin.
ask: Which anticoagulation response is most appropriate?
options: Stop all anticoagulation permanently because thrombocytopenia indicates spontaneous bleeding risk.
Stop all heparin exposure and seek haematology-guided therapeutic non-heparin anticoagulation.
Switch to prophylactic enoxaparin because it does not cross-react with heparin-associated antibodies.
Begin immediate warfarin alone at full dose before documenting the probability of HIT.
Give a platelet transfusion routinely and continue heparin until antibody tests are complete.
explanations: Stopping anticoagulation alone leaves a highly prothrombotic HIT state untreated. Platelet count reduction in HIT commonly coexists with new thrombosis.

Correct: this timing, substantial platelet decline and new DVT give high clinical suspicion for HIT. Discontinue UFH and LMWH, notify haematology, send appropriate immunological/functional tests, and start a therapeutic non-heparin anticoagulant unless contraindicated.
LMWH can cross-react with HIT antibodies and is not an appropriate substitute for UFH. A non-heparin agent such as argatroban or fondaparinux is chosen by clinical factors and specialist guidance.
Starting warfarin alone during acute HIT can worsen the thrombotic state and create risks such as limb gangrene. It is introduced later when safe and often after platelet recovery.

Routine platelet transfusion is generally avoided in HIT without serious bleeding or an indicated procedure, and continuing heparin can provoke further thrombosis. Test results do not need to precede action when suspicion is high.
pearl: A platelet fall five to ten days after heparin plus new thrombosis is HIT until urgently evaluated; stop both UFH and LMWH.
pivot: Isolated thrombocytopenia with a low clinical probability score and a clear alternate cause may not warrant empiric non-heparin anticoagulation.

steps: Calculate the 4Ts score and review heparin timing, nadir and newly documented thrombosis.
Stop all heparin products including line flushes and LMWH; document suspected HIT.
Initiate haematology-guided non-heparin therapeutic anticoagulation and monitor clot/bleeding status.
Send HIT immunoassay/functional tests, repeat platelets, and plan later transition when appropriate.
management.safety: Do not substitute enoxaparin for unfractionated heparin in suspected HIT or start warfarin monotherapy during acute HIT.
management.local: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand HIT consensus, with NSW Health 2024 protocol.

skill: Oesophageal button battery / removal within two hours
stem: A 20-month-old is brought to hospital after her parent saw her swallow a flat shiny object from a remote control. She is comfortable and swallowing normally. Two-view radiography identifies a 20-mm button battery lodged in the upper oesophagus. Estimated ingestion time was about an hour ago.
ask: Which intervention should take priority?
options: Discharge and ask parents to check stools because the child is not drooling or distressed.
Give several litres of oral fluid to wash the object into the stomach without intervention.
Arrange immediate specialist endoscopic removal, aiming for treatment within two hours of ingestion.
Plan repeat radiography after twenty-four hours because an oesophageal battery often passes spontaneously.
Attempt blind removal in the ED using fingers before involving paediatric gastroenterology or anaesthesia.
explanations: A lodged oesophageal button battery causes caustic injury through electrical current even in a comfortable child. Discharge is unsafe and serious damage may begin within two hours.
Oral fluids cannot reliably move an impacted button battery and may increase aspiration risk before anaesthesia. Appropriate treatment requires safe urgent removal.

Correct: activate paediatric gastroenterology/ENT, anaesthesia and resuscitation resources for time-critical endoscopic retrieval, with no delay for fasting. Follow specialist guidance on honey in a child over one year if ingestion was within twelve hours and airway is protected.
Waiting for migration risks deep oesophageal burns, tracheo-oesophageal injury and catastrophic haemorrhage. This high-risk location requires emergency action.
Blind retrieval can injure the airway or displace the battery. Removal belongs to an experienced airway/endoscopy team in a controlled environment.
pearl: A button battery in the oesophagus is a time-critical emergency—even if the child looks well—with removal ideally within two hours.
pivot: A battery already past the oesophagus and a completely asymptomatic child may follow a different specialist-directed observation or removal schedule depending on size and age.

steps: Obtain appropriate AP/lateral radiographs without delaying emergency specialist contact.
Call senior paediatric gastroenterology/ENT and anaesthesia for urgent endoscopy; do not delay for fasting.
Follow the local button-battery pathway, including specialist-directed honey when eligible while preparing removal.
Assess oesophageal injury and plan surveillance for delayed complications and prevention counselling.
management.safety: Do not wait for symptoms, attempt blind retrieval or prolong fasting before oesophageal battery removal.
management.local: RCH Foreign body ingestion guideline and Children's Health Queensland emergency battery pathway.

skill: Rabies exposure / category III prophylaxis in unvaccinated traveller
stem: A 29-year-old Australian traveller returns from a rabies-endemic country after a stray dog bit through the skin of her hand two days ago. She washed the wound briefly but received no vaccine. The dog cannot be found and she has no history of pre-exposure rabies vaccination or immunosuppression.
ask: Which prevention plan is most appropriate?
options: Observe for neurological symptoms because the dog has disappeared and cannot be laboratory tested.
Give rabies vaccine only, without immunoglobulin, because prophylaxis is ineffective after forty-eight hours.
Apply topical antibiotics and delay vaccination until a ten-day observation report is available.
Clean and assess the wound, then urgently arrange rabies vaccine plus human immunoglobulin.
Wait for rabies antibody testing to establish baseline immunity before deciding on any intervention.
explanations: A bite from an untraceable dog in a rabies-endemic area is not safely observed without post-exposure management. Once symptoms develop, rabies is almost universally fatal.
Unvaccinated people with category III transdermal exposure generally require both vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin. Forty-eight hours is not a reason to withhold prophylaxis.
The unavailable dog cannot be observed reliably, and topical wound treatment alone does not neutralise viral exposure. Delaying vaccination increases risk.

Correct: wash and irrigate the wound thoroughly, evaluate tetanus and bacterial infection, and immediately coordinate a category III Australian post-exposure regimen using rabies vaccine and HRIG infiltrated as advised.
Serology does not establish timely protection after a recent bite in an unvaccinated person, and awaiting it delays effective prevention. Follow the exposure-based PEP algorithm.
pearl: For an unvaccinated person with transdermal animal bite in a rabies-endemic area, vaccine PLUS HRIG are usually indicated; start PEP even when presentation is delayed.
pivot: A previously fully vaccinated immunocompetent traveller usually needs booster vaccine doses but not HRIG after a new exposure.

steps: Thoroughly wash/irrigate the wound, examine structures and manage bacterial infection/tetanus risk.
Confirm exposure category, animal location, immunisation history and availability for observation.
Urgently contact a public-health/infectious-diseases service for HRIG and recommended vaccine schedule.
Complete all scheduled vaccinations, check documentation and counsel on future avoidance.
management.safety: Do not wait for symptoms or withhold PEP because the bite was two days ago.
management.local: Australian Immunisation Handbook rabies post-exposure prophylaxis category-based guidance.

skill: Magnesium sulfate toxicity / reverse respiratory compromise
stem: A 32-year-old being treated with intravenous magnesium sulfate for pre-eclampsia becomes drowsy while receiving the maintenance infusion. Respiratory rate falls to 8/min, patellar reflexes are absent, oxygen saturation is 89% and urine output has fallen sharply. The clinical team has emergency calcium available.
ask: Which immediate management is most appropriate?
options: Increase the magnesium infusion because absent reflexes may indicate insufficient seizure prophylaxis.
Continue magnesium unchanged and obtain a level only after the scheduled next observation.
Administer additional antihypertensive therapy alone because poor respiratory effort is caused by hypertension.
Discontinue all monitoring if the blood pressure has reached the planned treatment range.
Stop magnesium, support ventilation and administer IV calcium gluconate with senior assistance.
explanations: Absent reflexes and respiratory depression indicate magnesium accumulation rather than inadequate seizure control. Increasing treatment can cause respiratory or cardiac arrest.
Waiting for a laboratory level in a patient with slowed breathing delays reversal of a clinically evident high-risk medicine toxicity.
BP treatment remains important in pre-eclampsia, but antihypertensives do not reverse magnesium-related neuromuscular depression. Airway and antidote treatment are immediate priorities.
Normalization of BP does not guarantee safe magnesium exposure, especially with decreased renal elimination. Observations must intensify, not stop.

Correct: stop the infusion immediately, summon obstetric/anaesthetic help, support oxygenation and ventilation, and give protocol-guided IV calcium gluconate for significant respiratory toxicity while assessing renal function and magnesium concentration.
pearl: Loss of tendon reflexes with slow breathing during magnesium infusion is toxicity; stop the infusion and reverse serious respiratory depression with calcium.
pivot: Mild flushing or nausea with preserved reflexes, breathing and urine output may be a non-toxic adverse effect and needs assessment but not automatically calcium antidote.

steps: Immediately halt magnesium sulfate and activate emergency obstetric/anaesthetic response.
Check respiratory effort and oxygenation, administer oxygen and ventilatory support as required.
Administer IV calcium gluconate using local protocol with continuous monitoring.
Recheck magnesium, renal function and urine output; reassess safe pre-eclampsia seizure prophylaxis.
management.safety: Magnesium is a high-risk medicine; absent reflexes or respiratory rate below 12/min requires urgent escalation.
management.local: Queensland Clinical Guidelines Hypertension and pregnancy: Magnesium sulfate protocol (2025).

skill: Refractory anaphylaxis / escalation beyond intramuscular adrenaline
stem: A 29-year-old develops throat tightness, widespread urticaria and collapse after eating cashews. Two appropriately administered intramuscular adrenaline doses five minutes apart and initial fluid resuscitation have not resolved wheezing or hypotension. BP is 75/40 mmHg, with a weak peripheral pulse. A senior emergency team is present.
ask: What is the best immediate escalation while continuing resuscitation?
options: Commence a monitored IV adrenaline infusion under experienced resuscitation supervision.
Administer IV chlorphenamine as the primary intervention for ongoing cardiovascular collapse.
Give an additional dose of systemic corticosteroid and await its onset of action.
Use nebulised salbutamol alone because persistent wheeze identifies isolated bronchospasm.
Arrange urgent imaging of the neck to quantify upper-airway oedema before further treatment.
explanations: Correct: persistent respiratory or cardiovascular compromise after two IM doses constitutes refractory anaphylaxis. Expert-guided IV adrenaline infusion, repeated fluid assessment and advanced airway readiness address the continuing life threat.
Antihistamines may relieve skin symptoms later, but do not reliably reverse distributive shock or critical airway swelling. IV antihistamine administration may itself worsen haemodynamics.
Corticosteroids act too slowly to treat shock and are not routine first-line anaphylaxis therapy. Their use as an adjunct in selected refractory cases must not interrupt adrenaline resuscitation.
Nebulised beta-agonists can supplement treatment of bronchospasm, but cannot restore vascular tone or reliably treat anaphylactic airway oedema and hypotension.
Imaging neither diagnoses nor treats anaphylactic shock. A rapidly evolving airway problem requires clinical reassessment and expert intervention rather than transport to radiology.
pearl: Persistent hypotension or breathing difficulty after two IM adrenaline doses defines refractory anaphylaxis; escalate to expert-supervised IV adrenaline.
pivot: If symptoms improve promptly after initial IM adrenaline and blood pressure normalises, continue observation and trigger-avoidance planning rather than an IV infusion.

steps: Activate resuscitation, request airway and senior emergency expertise, and continuously monitor ECG, pressure and oxygenation.
Continue IM adrenaline per protocol while an experienced team establishes carefully titrated IV adrenaline infusion and assesses additional crystalloid.
Prepare for early advanced airway management if stridor, swelling or ventilatory failure advances.
Monitor for recurrent symptoms; document trigger and arrange adrenaline autoinjector education and allergy referral.
management.safety: Never give unsupervised IV adrenaline boluses for routine anaphylaxis; medication concentration and infusion titration require resuscitation-level checks.
management.local: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10 (July 2026), refractory anaphylaxis.

skill: Decompensated cirrhosis / spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
stem: A 58-year-old with known cirrhosis and tense ascites is admitted with increasing confusion and abdominal discomfort. He has no guarding and is afebrile, but diagnostic paracentesis shows an ascitic neutrophil count of 420 cells/µL. Cultures are pending. BP is 104/62 mmHg and creatinine is mildly elevated.
ask: Which next treatment most directly addresses the likely diagnosis and prevents deterioration?
options: Repeat paracentesis after three days to confirm the neutrophil threshold before giving antimicrobials.
Start empirical IV antibiotics for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and assess albumin indications.
Treat only hepatic encephalopathy with lactulose because the patient has no fever or peritonism.
Begin routine prophylactic oral antibiotics rather than therapeutic dosing because cultures are pending.
Perform therapeutic paracentesis alone to remove infected fluid and reassess the renal function.
explanations: An ascitic polymorphonuclear count at or above 250 cells/µL is sufficient for presumptive SBP, even without positive culture. Delaying antibiotics risks sepsis and renal failure.

Correct: treat culture-negative neutrocytic ascites as SBP, obtain blood and ascitic cultures, provide empirical systemic antibiotics adapted to local resistance, and consider IV albumin in renal dysfunction or other high-risk features.
Hepatic encephalopathy may coexist or be precipitated by infection. Lactulose can be appropriate, but leaving SBP untreated risks worsening brain function, kidney injury and death.
Secondary prophylaxis is considered after completing active treatment; preventive-dose antibiotics do not adequately treat confirmed neutrocytic ascites.
Large-volume drainage may relieve tense ascites, but is not adequate infection treatment. Monitor haemodynamics and consider volume replacement when large volumes are removed.
pearl: SBP is diagnosed by ascitic neutrophils of at least 250/µL; fever, peritoneal tenderness and culture positivity are not required.
pivot: A neutrophil count below diagnostic threshold with a stable patient may lead to other infection investigation and culture-guided decisions, rather than automatic SBP therapy.

steps: Treat the ascitic neutrophil result as an infection; repeat ABCDE and evaluate encephalopathy, sepsis and renal status.
Send ascitic fluid and blood cultures promptly without postponing antibiotic administration.
Start local-protocol empirical IV antibiotics; review IV albumin eligibility and nephrotoxic medicines.
Monitor creatinine, urine output, symptoms and inflammatory response; plan secondary prophylaxis after recovery.
management.safety: A normal temperature or absent guarding does not safely exclude life-threatening SBP in a person with cirrhosis.
management.local: Australian Gastroenterology Society guidance and local inpatient SBP protocol.

skill: Acute cholangitis / septic shock and biliary source control
stem: A 72-year-old with known gallstones is febrile and jaundiced with right upper-quadrant pain. BP is 83/47 mmHg after initial crystalloid, lactate is 4.2 mmol/L, bilirubin is elevated and ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct. The surgical registrar asks whether to wait for MRCP before arranging a procedure.
ask: What is the best next management priority?
options: Obtain an elective MRCP first because noninvasive duct imaging should always precede treatment.
Schedule laparoscopic cholecystectomy after several days of antibiotics to remove the underlying gallstones.
Resuscitate and give antibiotics while arranging urgent biliary decompression through the specialist team.
Offer analgesia and repeat liver tests because some stones pass spontaneously without intervention.
Transfer for outpatient ERCP once lactate normalises on IV fluids and oral antibiotics.
explanations: MRCP can define obstruction in stable diagnostic uncertainty but must not postpone source control for shock with likely ascending cholangitis. The ultrasound and clinical picture are sufficient for urgent escalation.
Cholecystectomy addresses gallbladder stones but does not relieve an infected obstructed common duct in the acute shock phase. Definitive gallbladder management can follow stabilisation.

Correct: activate sepsis management with timely IV antimicrobials, haemodynamic support and urgent gastroenterology/surgery referral for ERCP drainage or an alternative decompression approach. Organ support and source control proceed together.
Stone passage is possible but is an unsafe assumption in a patient with persistent hypotension and lactic acidosis. Symptomatic care alone leaves ongoing biliary sepsis untreated.
Outpatient care is inappropriate after shock physiology. IV fluids may transiently improve circulation without resolving the infected obstruction that sustains severe illness.
pearl: Severe cholangitis is simultaneously a sepsis problem and an obstructed-duct problem: antibiotics without drainage may fail.
pivot: An afebrile stable patient with biliary colic and no systemic inflammation or duct obstruction follows an elective gallstone assessment pathway.

steps: Call senior ED/ICU assistance, monitor perfusion and give titrated IV fluids and vasopressors when necessary.
Draw cultures if promptly available and administer local guideline IV broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Discuss urgent ERCP decompression with gastroenterology; plan percutaneous or surgical drainage if ERCP fails.
Monitor lactate, kidney function, bilirubin, coagulation and clinical response; address gallbladder management after recovery.
management.safety: Do not delay drainage in septic shock for additional elective imaging or a trial of oral medication.
management.local: Use local Australian biliary sepsis and endoscopy emergency pathways.

skill: Open tibial fracture / antibiotic timing and surgical debridement
stem: A 34-year-old motorcyclist arrives after a crash with a deformed lower leg. A 5-cm contaminated wound exposes the tibial shaft, distal pulses are palpable and the leg is sensate. Trauma imaging shows a displaced open fracture. The ED team can deliver IV antibiotics immediately; orthopaedic theatre is expected in several hours.
ask: What is the safest immediate management combination?
options: Irrigate deeply in the emergency bay, close the skin primarily and apply a walking cast.
Defer antibiotics until deep operative samples have identified the likely contaminating bacteria.
Wait for the orthopaedic consultant before applying any dressing or immobilising the limb.
Give prompt IV antibiotics, cover the wound, splint and arrange urgent operative debridement.
Discharge with oral antibiotics and protected weight bearing because distal circulation is preserved.
explanations: Definitive wound debridement and closure strategy require theatre assessment. Aggressive bedside exploration or closure can trap contamination and worsen soft tissue damage.
Antibiotic administration early after an open fracture reduces infection risk; delaying for culture is not justified. Operative specimens can be obtained later if infection is suspected.
Senior input is important but temporising sterile wound coverage and immobilisation should start at once. Delay adds pain, bleeding and soft-tissue injury without benefit.

Correct: follow trauma ABCs, document neurovascular status and compartment findings, start protocol-based IV antibiotics promptly, cover with a sterile dressing, splint and arrange specialist theatre washout/debridement and fixation. Update tetanus status.
A normal pulse does not make an exposed contaminated fracture safe for outpatient treatment. Infection, soft-tissue injury and compartment syndrome remain major threats.
pearl: For an open fracture, early systemic antibiotics and safe immobilisation begin before theatre; debridement and closure are specialist procedures.
pivot: A closed, stable fracture with intact neurovascular findings may follow immobilisation and outpatient fracture-clinic review if specialist criteria are satisfied.

steps: Assess other injuries, analgesia, haemorrhage, distal motor/sensation/perfusion and emerging compartment syndrome.
Gently cover the wound with sterile dressing, maintain limb alignment and splint without forcing reduction.
Administer immediate IV antibiotics based on local open-fracture protocol and tetanus prophylaxis when appropriate.
Arrange orthopaedic and plastic surgery review for debridement, fixation and wound coverage planning.
management.safety: Check and document neurovascular examination before and after splinting; deterioration suggests vascular compromise or compartment syndrome.
management.local: Australian orthopaedic trauma and local open-fracture antibiotic pathways.

skill: Central retinal artery occlusion / stroke-equivalent
stem: A 67-year-old with atrial fibrillation suddenly loses vision in the right eye while reading. He has no pain, conjunctival redness or flashes. Visual acuity is reduced to hand movements, and fundus examination suggests retinal arterial whitening and a cherry-red macular spot. Symptom onset was 55 minutes ago.
ask: What is the most appropriate immediate pathway?
options: Arrange a routine optometry review because painless monocular vision loss is rarely an emergency.
Treat presumed acute glaucoma empirically because sudden severe visual loss requires lowering pressure.
Order an outpatient carotid Doppler after initial antiplatelet treatment without emergency assessment.
Observe for spontaneous recovery and re-evaluate vision after the atrial fibrillation rate is controlled.
Activate an acute stroke and ophthalmology pathway for urgent time-sensitive vascular assessment.
explanations: CRAO threatens permanent vision and is associated with concurrent or subsequent cerebral ischaemia. Routine optometry is too slow for an onset measured in minutes.
Angle-closure glaucoma usually causes pain, red eye, headache and often a raised intraocular pressure. CRAO needs neurovascular evaluation rather than assuming a pressure-mediated process.
Carotid investigation is relevant but a future appointment misses a potentially time-sensitive intervention and immediate assessment of cardioembolic and cerebrovascular risk.
Some visual recovery occurs, but observation wastes the very narrow therapeutic opportunity. Rate control alone does not treat an acute retinal arterial occlusion.

Correct: treat retinal arterial occlusion as an acute ischaemic emergency with urgent stroke-team and ophthalmology involvement, vascular and cardiac assessment and discussion of reperfusion eligibility according to specialised local protocols.
pearl: Sudden painless monocular visual loss from CRAO is an eye emergency and a stroke-equivalent requiring immediate coordinated assessment.
pivot: Transient monocular visual obscuration with complete recovery suggests amaurosis fugax, which still requires urgent TIA/stroke investigation.

steps: Document last-known-well time, visual findings, vascular risk factors and medication including anticoagulants.
Urgently involve stroke and ophthalmology teams and send for emergency brain and vascular investigation as directed.
Discuss time-dependent reperfusion eligibility and exclusions with the responsible specialists.
Investigate atrial fibrillation, carotid disease and vascular risks, then implement tailored secondary prevention.
management.safety: Do not delay urgent referral for non-evidence-based globe massage or routine outpatient tests.
management.local: Stroke Foundation Australia and local acute retinal artery occlusion emergency pathway.

skill: Acute limb ischaemia / limb-saving referral
stem: A 71-year-old with atrial fibrillation stopped apixaban for a dental procedure three days ago. He suddenly develops severe left-foot pain and tingling. The leg is pale and cold below the knee, with absent pedal Doppler signals and reduced toe sensation. The right leg is warm with palpable pulses.
ask: Which immediate plan best preserves limb viability?
options: Give analgesia, initiate urgent vascular consultation and consider IV heparin after contraindication review.
Request a routine outpatient duplex scan before deciding whether anticoagulation is required.
Treat for deep venous thrombosis with compression stockings and review pulses after mobilisation.
Start oral antibiotics for possible cellulitis and obtain repeated inflammatory markers before referral.
Place the limb above heart level and arrange a repeat examination on the following morning.
explanations: Correct: six-P features suggest an acute embolic arterial occlusion with a threatened limb. Obtain urgent vascular input, document motor/sensory deficit and start anticoagulation when appropriate under protocol while preparing revascularisation.
Outpatient imaging is too slow in a limb whose nerve and muscle function may deteriorate over hours. Specialist-directed vascular imaging should not delay escalation.
DVT generally causes swelling and warmth, not a suddenly cold pulseless leg. Compression is not an adequate response to arterial occlusion.
Cellulitis does not explain loss of arterial signals and abrupt paraesthesia. Antibiotic treatment without restoring perfusion risks tissue necrosis.
Elevation can further reduce perfusion to an ischaemic limb. Reassessment the next day is unsafe when neurological changes and absent arterial flow are already present.
pearl: A cold, painful, pulseless limb with altered sensation is time-critical arterial ischaemia until proven otherwise.
pivot: A chronically diminished pulse without acute pain, coldness or new neurological findings may be managed through a chronic peripheral arterial disease pathway.

steps: Compare limbs and document the six Ps, motor power, sensory changes and Doppler signals.
Contact vascular surgery and emergency retrieval immediately; do not wait for routine imaging.
Provide analgesia, vascular access and specialist-directed IV heparin after bleeding contraindications are reviewed.
Arrange urgent imaging/revascularisation and monitor for reperfusion injury and compartment syndrome.
management.safety: Do not elevate a profoundly ischaemic limb or postpone vascular assessment while arranging outpatient tests.
management.local: Queensland Health Primary Clinical Care Manual: acute lower-leg ischaemia.

skill: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia / seizures
stem: A 60-year-old taking hydrochlorothiazide is brought in after a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure. She remains confused, sodium is 112 mmol/L and glucose is normal. Her partner reports progressive nausea and headache for two days. The emergency registrar worries that all sodium correction must be very slow.
ask: What is the safest priority during this neurological emergency?
options: Restrict water and defer any active correction until a repeat morning sodium level.
Administer protocol-based hypertonic saline for seizures with close neurological and sodium monitoring.
Give a large volume of hypotonic fluid to avoid overly rapid changes in serum osmolality.
Continue hydrochlorothiazide and treat the convulsion alone until the patient becomes fully alert.
Give oral salt tablets and observe because seizures can occur independently of hyponatraemia.
explanations: Water restriction can help selected stable forms of hyponatraemia, but convulsions require prompt controlled hypertonic treatment to reduce cerebral oedema.

Correct: emergency hypertonic saline is indicated in severe neurological symptoms, alongside airway/seizure management. Measure sodium frequently and use a tightly controlled correction plan to avoid overcorrection after initial stabilisation.
Hypotonic fluid may lower sodium further and worsen cerebral swelling. Fluid prescription must reflect neurologic severity and actual volume status.
Thiazides can precipitate hyponatraemia and should be withheld. Treating convulsions alone ignores the underlying metabolic trigger.
Oral tablets cannot reliably treat cerebral oedema quickly, and oral administration is unsafe during confusion or impaired airway protection.
pearl: Seizures from hyponatraemia justify an urgent limited rise in sodium, followed by careful prevention of overcorrection.
pivot: Chronic mild hyponatraemia without neurological symptoms may be addressed with cause correction and a slower sodium strategy.

steps: Manage airway and seizures, call critical-care support, and check repeat glucose and electrolytes.
Use monitored hypertonic saline per local severe-symptomatic-hyponatraemia protocol.
Monitor sodium and urine output frequently and avoid excessive total daily correction.
Stop thiazides, assess volume status and other triggers, and involve endocrinology/nephrology if needed.
management.safety: A rapid initial emergency rise must not become uncontrolled prolonged correction; osmotic demyelination is a risk.
management.local: Queensland Health 2026 electrolyte disturbances prescribing guidelines for adults, severe symptomatic hyponatraemia.

skill: Necrotising soft-tissue infection / operative source control
stem: A 48-year-old with diabetes has rapidly progressive erythema of the thigh after a minor abrasion. Pain is extreme despite little surface change. She is febrile, tachycardic and develops purple patches and reduced skin sensation within hours. Lactate is 3.8 mmol/L and BP is 92/54 mmHg.
ask: Which management pathway best addresses the threat?
options: Book MRI first and wait for the report before involving surgeons in the case.
Start an oral antibiotic and review the area after twenty-four hours of elevation.
Activate sepsis resuscitation, urgent surgical exploration and broad empirical IV antibiotics.
Perform bedside superficial incision and drainage, then discharge once pain is controlled.
Wait for positive blood cultures before choosing whether operative debridement is justified.
explanations: Imaging may support diagnosis in uncertain stable cases, but rapidly progressive shock and disproportionate pain mandate urgent surgical assessment; imaging must not delay debridement.
Oral antibiotics and short-interval outpatient follow-up are inadequate for suspected necrotising infection, which may advance rapidly through deep tissues.

Correct: resuscitate sepsis, involve senior surgery and intensive care immediately, give broad IV antibiotics including toxin-suppressing cover as guided locally, and proceed to urgent exploration and debridement.
Superficial drainage cannot remove deep fascial necrosis. A reassuring surface appearance or transient analgesic response is not evidence of adequate source control.
Cultures are useful for later antibiotic targeting, but awaiting results postpones lifesaving source control. Necrotising infection remains a clinical and surgical diagnosis.
pearl: Pain out of proportion, rapid progression and systemic toxicity suggest necrotising infection even before obvious crepitus.
pivot: A stable, slowly developing superficial abscess without systemic toxicity can often be managed with local drainage and tailored outpatient follow-up.

steps: Activate the sepsis pathway, repeat observations, secure access and restore perfusion.
Request immediate surgical and ICU assessment; do not delay for radiology.
Obtain cultures if feasible and administer local-protocol broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.
Arrange urgent extensive surgical exploration/debridement with repeat review as needed.
management.safety: An unremarkable early scan or blood test cannot reliably exclude necrotising fasciitis.
management.local: Australian emergency sepsis and necrotising soft-tissue infection pathways.

skill: Massive pulmonary embolism / shock and reperfusion
stem: A 49-year-old develops abrupt pleuritic chest pain, severe breathlessness and near-syncope two weeks after hip surgery. BP is 72/44 mmHg, SpO2 85% and bedside echocardiography shows an enlarged struggling right ventricle. CT pulmonary angiography cannot be obtained without substantial delay; bleeding risk is elevated because of the recent surgery.
ask: What should be prioritised in this unstable presentation?
options: Transfer immediately for outpatient imaging because the diagnosis is not yet definite.
Give a large litre bolus repeatedly until the systolic pressure stays over 120 mmHg.
Treat presumed pneumonia empirically and reassess the right ventricle after antibiotic response.
Activate critical care and PE specialists for urgent reperfusion decisions alongside stabilisation.
Withhold all anticoagulation until a CT scan has documented a filling defect.
explanations: Outpatient investigation is unsafe in profound circulatory collapse. Cardiogenic shock from pulmonary vascular obstruction can progress to cardiac arrest.
Indiscriminate large fluid loads may worsen right ventricular dilatation and reduce cardiac output. Small cautious resuscitation and vasoactive support may be preferable.
Infection can cause hypoxia, but sudden onset, recent surgery, severe hypotension and RV strain make high-risk PE a key emergency. Antibiotics alone will not relieve obstruction.

Correct: involve ICU, emergency medicine and a multidisciplinary PE/reperfusion team urgently, stabilise oxygenation and RV perfusion, and weigh systemic thrombolysis against catheter-based or surgical options given recent surgery.

CTPA is valuable but the patient may be too unstable for transport. Management can be guided by bedside echocardiography and specialist assessment when definitive imaging would dangerously delay care.
pearl: Hypotensive suspected PE with acute RV dysfunction needs emergency reperfusion planning, not routine ward anticoagulation alone.
pivot: A haemodynamically stable patient with low or moderate PE probability can follow a structured testing pathway with D-dimer or imaging.

steps: Give oxygen, monitor ECG and haemodynamics, avoid excessive fluids and use vasoactive support when indicated.
Activate senior critical care, cardiology/respiratory and reperfusion specialists immediately.
Assess urgent anticoagulation and systemic or procedural reperfusion according to bleeding risks and local capabilities.
Reassess RV function, oxygenation and recurrent shock; investigate DVT and longer-term anticoagulation needs.
management.safety: Recent surgery increases bleeding hazard and may change reperfusion modality; make this a specialist emergency decision.
management.local: Australian and New Zealand acute pulmonary embolism and ICU management pathways.

skill: Febrile neutropenia / prompt empirical antibiotics
stem: A 59-year-old receiving chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia presents with temperature 38.7°C and mild sore throat. Neutrophils are 0.2 × 10⁹/L. HR is 118/min, BP 110/66 mmHg and he has no focal examination findings. The ED is busy, and a blood culture courier will not arrive for an hour.
ask: What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Discharge with oral antibiotics and review tomorrow because blood pressure remains preserved.
Wait for central and peripheral culture results before starting any antimicrobial therapy.
Give antipyretics and repeat the full blood count after the temperature has settled.
Administer growth factor alone because the low neutrophil count is the primary problem.
Start immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and urgent sepsis/oncology assessment without culture delay.
explanations: Profound neutropenia plus fever after chemotherapy is a medical emergency with rapid invasive bacterial infection risk. Stable early BP is not enough for outpatient reassurance.
Collect cultures promptly when feasible, but their results take much longer than the safe treatment window. Empirical therapy must not wait for culture availability.
Antipyretics improve comfort but can obscure fever and do not treat infection risk. Monitoring without antimicrobials is inappropriate.
G-CSF may be indicated in selected oncology situations but does not replace empiric antimicrobial treatment for an acute febrile neutropenic episode.

Correct: initiate a neutropenic sepsis pathway, obtain appropriate cultures and give timely antipseudomonal IV antibiotics according to local resistance and allergy history, with senior oncology input and admission.
pearl: Fever with profound chemotherapy-associated neutropenia is an antibiotic emergency even without a localising source.
pivot: An immunocompetent adult with low-grade fever and normal neutrophils follows risk-based assessment rather than automatic high-risk neutropenic cover.

steps: Recognise chemotherapy-related neutropenic infection, assess sepsis and establish IV access.
Send blood cultures and required bloods rapidly; do not defer treatment if specimen collection is delayed.
Give prompt empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics with local antipseudomonal cover and fluid support as needed.
Contact haematology/oncology and admit for monitoring, reassessment and culture-led antibiotic adjustment.
management.safety: Do not delay the first antibiotic dose to wait for imaging, blood culture transport or an obvious infection focus.
management.local: eviQ endorsed Australasian neutropenic fever assessment and initial antimicrobial guidance, v7.

skill: Haemophilia A / head trauma before imaging
stem: A 9-year-old with severe haemophilia A strikes his head falling from a bicycle. He is alert, has vomited once and reports worsening headache. He has no focal deficit and last received prophylactic factor VIII four days ago. The CT scanner is available, but the haemophilia nurse has brought his emergency factor supply.
ask: Which sequence is safest while investigating possible intracranial bleeding?
options: Give indicated factor VIII promptly with specialist advice, then pursue urgent CT and observation.
Complete CT and coagulation studies first, giving factor VIII only if bleeding is demonstrated.
Provide analgesia and discharge if his neurological examination remains normal for one hour.
Administer vitamin K immediately, because haemophilia-related bleeding responds to clotting-factor synthesis.
Perform lumbar puncture to exclude subarachnoid bleeding before prescribing clotting-factor replacement.
explanations: Correct: suspected serious bleeding in haemophilia requires immediate appropriate factor replacement; imaging must not delay it. Worsening headache and vomiting also require urgent CT and haematology-led observation.
Intracranial bleeding can progress during imaging and laboratory delays. Factor levels can support subsequent dosing but must not hold up initial treatment.
An initially normal examination does not exclude intracranial haemorrhage. Brief observation without replacement and investigation is unsafe in severe haemophilia with progressive symptoms.
Vitamin K supports vitamin-K-dependent factors, whereas haemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency. It does not provide the replacement needed for this inherited condition.
Lumbar puncture risks further bleeding and is not the initial test for traumatic intracranial haemorrhage. Invasive procedures require a specialist haemostatic plan.
pearl: In haemophilia with suspected major bleeding, replace factor first and investigate in parallel.
pivot: A known factor VIII inhibitor or emicizumab prophylaxis changes specialist haemostatic product selection.

steps: Assess ABCDE, cervical injury risk and serial neurological observations.
Call the haemophilia centre and administer indicated factor replacement immediately.
Arrange urgent head CT and appropriate blood tests without treatment delay.
Arrange observation and neurosurgical review if intracranial bleeding is found.
management.safety: Ask about inhibitors and emicizumab because they alter product choice and some coagulation assays.
management.local: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Haemophilia guideline.

skill: Immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis / early immunosuppression
stem: A 64-year-old receiving nivolumab for metastatic melanoma develops fatigue, chest pressure and palpitations five weeks after treatment began. Troponin is elevated and ECG shows new conduction delay. Coronary assessment does not support an acute plaque event, and echocardiography reports a preserved ejection fraction. The next nivolumab infusion is booked tomorrow.
ask: What is the most appropriate response to this treatment-related concern?
options: Proceed with the next infusion and review symptoms after the planned treatment cycle.
Withhold immunotherapy and admit for monitored cardio-oncology assessment and prompt corticosteroid treatment.
Discharge with a beta blocker because preserved ejection fraction excludes clinically important myocarditis.
Delay management until cardiac MRI proves myocarditis because troponin elevation alone is nonspecific.
Give an NSAID and resume exercise because treatment-related pericarditis is more likely than myocarditis.
explanations: Continuing a suspected immune trigger can worsen fatal cardiac toxicity. Even mild early symptoms warrant withholding treatment and urgent assessment.

Correct: immune checkpoint myocarditis may cause malignant arrhythmias despite normal LV function. Hold treatment, admit for telemetry, involve specialists and start early high-dose corticosteroids per protocol.
Normal ejection fraction does not exclude myocarditis or conduction-related sudden death. Troponin elevation with new ECG changes warrants hospital evaluation.
MRI can help confirm myocarditis, but should not postpone stabilisation or prompt treatment when suspicion is high. Investigate competing causes concurrently.
NSAIDs may help selected pericardial syndromes but are not adequate for suspected myocardial inflammation with conduction abnormalities.
pearl: Checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis can be fatal even when ejection fraction is preserved.
pivot: A convincingly established alternative cause of troponin elevation changes treatment, but must be demonstrated rather than assumed.

steps: Stop further nivolumab and alert the oncology team.
Admit with telemetry, serial ECG/troponin, BNP, CK and echocardiography.
Seek urgent cardiology advice and begin early high-dose IV corticosteroids per irAE protocol.
Consider cardiac MRI, conduction complications and associated myositis.
management.safety: Normal EF is not reassuring; avoid infliximab in myocarditis or heart failure.
management.local: eviQ Management of immune-related adverse events v6, cardiac toxicity.

skill: Organophosphate exposure / atropine endpoints
stem: A 38-year-old agricultural worker is brought in after mixing insecticide in an enclosed shed. He is sweating heavily, salivating, wheezing and passing diarrhoea. HR is 54/min and SpO2 is 86% despite oxygen. Pinpoint pupils and diffuse bronchial secretions are noted. Contaminated clothing is still on his body.
ask: Which intervention should be prioritised to reverse the immediately dangerous toxidrome?
options: Give naloxone until pupil size normalises, then begin environmental decontamination.
Administer activated charcoal before airway support because the agent is a pesticide.
Use escalating IV atropine to clear bronchial secretions while providing protected decontamination.
Give flumazenil to improve respiratory effort while awaiting confirmation of the insecticide.
Provide pralidoxime alone because muscarinic symptoms should settle once enzyme activity recovers.
explanations: Naloxone treats opioid toxicity, not organophosphate-mediated bronchorrhoea or bradycardia. It cannot replace cholinergic antidote therapy.
Activated charcoal does not address inhaled or dermal exposure and is dangerous with respiratory compromise. Airway support and staff protection come first.
Correct: atropine is rapidly titrated to clear lung secretions and improve ventilation/perfusion, not pupil size. Use PPE, remove clothing and discuss pralidoxime with toxicology.
Flumazenil reverses selected benzodiazepine effects, not acetylcholinesterase inhibition, and may precipitate seizures in mixed poisonings.
Pralidoxime can assist in selected cases but does not replace immediate atropine for muscarinic respiratory failure. Airway support is also critical.
pearl: Titrate atropine to clear the lungs, not to dilate pupils.
pivot: Dry skin, mydriasis and urinary retention suggest anticholinergic toxicity, not cholinergic excess.

steps: Use PPE and remove contaminated clothing without exposing staff.
Suction secretions, give oxygen and secure ventilation as required.
Administer escalating IV atropine with repeated chest and perfusion assessment.
Call Poisons Information 13 11 26 about oximes and ongoing infusion.
management.safety: Secondary contamination can harm staff; heart rate and pupil size are not sole atropinisation endpoints.
management.local: Queensland Poisons Information Centre atropine guidance.

skill: Meningococcal contact management / targeted prophylaxis
stem: A 19-year-old university student has confirmed invasive meningococcal disease. His asymptomatic housemate slept in the same shared bedroom for the preceding week. Several classmates attended the same lecture but had no close social contact. The housemate completed meningococcal vaccinations during school.
ask: Which action is most appropriate for the asymptomatic housemate?
options: Reassure because childhood vaccination removes the need for any further contact management.
Order a throat culture and prescribe antibiotics only if meningococcal carriage is confirmed.
Give prophylaxis only if fever develops because antibiotic treatment is unnecessary while asymptomatic.
Arrange prompt clearance antibiotics through public health, regardless of prior vaccination status.
Vaccinate the entire lecture group urgently instead of treating those with household-level exposure.
explanations: Vaccination reduces disease risk but does not remove the need for prophylaxis after defined high-risk exposure. Carriage and vaccine serogroup coverage are distinct issues.
Carriage testing is not needed to determine eligibility for chemoprophylaxis. Waiting for a throat culture can miss the prevention window.
Chemoprophylaxis prevents secondary disease in asymptomatic high-risk contacts. Waiting for fever converts prevention into urgent treatment.
Correct: household-like contact warrants prompt public-health-coordinated clearance antibiotics, plus serogroup-specific vaccine advice where appropriate.
Routine lecture attendance does not equal household-level exposure. Blanket antibiotics or vaccination for casual classmates can cause avoidable harm.
pearl: Meningococcal prophylaxis is determined by exposure, not symptoms or previous vaccination.
pivot: A classmate who only shared lectures without close contact generally needs information and safety advice, not automatic antibiotics.

steps: Confirm public health notification and contact tracing.
Identify household, intimate and other defined high-risk contacts.
Give clearance antibiotics promptly using local drug and pregnancy guidance.
Explain symptoms requiring urgent care and vaccine indications.
management.safety: Do not await symptoms or throat cultures in high-risk contacts; casual contacts usually do not need prophylaxis.
management.local: NSW Health meningococcal disease control guideline.

skill: Tumour lysis syndrome / rasburicase contraindication
stem: A 25-year-old with bulky Burkitt lymphoma is scheduled for intensive chemotherapy. LDH is markedly elevated, urate is already high and eGFR is reduced. The oncology registrar proposes allopurinol alone with unrestricted oral fluids. The patient has a documented history of G6PD deficiency.
ask: Which prevention plan best addresses the high risk while respecting the contraindication?
options: Start rasburicase immediately because renal dysfunction outweighs the risk from G6PD deficiency.
Give allopurinol and rasburicase together because dual urate blockade is recommended in high-risk disease.
Defer all prophylaxis until chemotherapy produces laboratory evidence of tumour lysis syndrome.
Give oral sodium bicarbonate routinely because urinary alkalinisation prevents calcium-phosphate deposition.
Institute monitored IV hydration and specialist urate-lowering planning without rasburicase in G6PD deficiency.
explanations: Rasburicase can cause haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in G6PD deficiency. High TLS risk does not remove this contraindication.
eviQ does not recommend routine combined allopurinol and rasburicase. Rasburicase is contraindicated here regardless of concurrent allopurinol.
Prevention must begin before cytotoxic therapy for high-risk disease. Waiting for renal failure or arrhythmia loses the opportunity to prevent TLS.
Routine urinary alkalinisation can increase calcium-phosphate precipitation and is not recommended. Hydration and safe urate management are preferred.

Correct: initiate monitored hydration, frequent electrolyte/urate testing and urgent haematology-nephrology planning. Consider renal-adjusted allopurinol while avoiding rasburicase in G6PD deficiency.
pearl: Rasburicase is effective for high-risk TLS but contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.
pivot: In G6PD-normal high-risk patients, rasburicase may be appropriate with specialist oversight.

steps: Review tumour burden, LDH, urate, renal function and treatment intensity.
Use carefully titrated IV fluids with strict balance and monitoring.
Avoid rasburicase in G6PD deficiency; plan alternative urate management with specialists.
Monitor potassium, phosphate, calcium and renal function; escalate for dialysis if needed.
management.safety: Do not administer rasburicase in G6PD deficiency or routinely alkalinise urine.
management.local: eviQ Prevention of tumour lysis syndrome.

skill: Sickle cell disease / acute chest syndrome
stem: A 12-year-old with HbSS disease is admitted for a painful vaso-occlusive episode. The next morning he develops fever, cough and chest pain. SpO2 falls from 98% to 91% on room air, and radiography shows a new right lower-zone infiltrate. His haemoglobin is near baseline and he remains haemodynamically stable.
ask: What is the safest immediate management bundle?
options: Treat acute chest syndrome with oxygen, IV antibiotics, careful fluids and urgent haematology input.
Increase maintenance IV fluids to twice normal because hydration alone reverses pulmonary sickling.
Give opioids only and repeat the chest radiograph in two days if pain persists.
Arrange routine outpatient respiratory review because haemoglobin has not fallen below baseline.
Start anticoagulation for presumed pulmonary embolism without evaluating the new pulmonary infiltrate.
explanations: Correct: a new infiltrate with hypoxia and respiratory symptoms indicates acute chest syndrome. Provide oxygen, early antibiotics, analgesia and cautious hydration; involve haematology regarding transfusion and critical-care escalation.
Excessive IV fluids can worsen acute chest syndrome. Correct true dehydration but avoid reflexively doubling fluid rates in a patient with pulmonary compromise.
Analgesia is important but cannot replace treatment of hypoxia and possible infection. Waiting two days risks rapid respiratory deterioration.
A haemoglobin near baseline does not exclude acute chest syndrome. New oxygen requirement and infiltrate warrant inpatient care regardless of initial haemodynamic stability.
PE may be a differential but empiric anticoagulation without appropriate assessment misses the characteristic acute chest presentation and adds bleeding risk.
pearl: Acute chest syndrome may develop during a pain crisis even without an early haemoglobin drop.
pivot: Isolated limb pain without fever, hypoxia or new chest infiltrate supports uncomplicated vaso-occlusive pain management.

steps: Repeat SpO2, examination, chest imaging, FBC/reticulocytes and cultures if febrile.
Give oxygen, adequate analgesia and respiratory monitoring.
Start protocol-based IV antibiotics and carefully balanced fluids.
Seek haematology and critical-care review; assess transfusion if deteriorating.
management.safety: Avoid fluid overload and excessive transfusion targets because of pulmonary deterioration and hyperviscosity risk.
management.local: Perth Children's Hospital Sickle cell disease ED guideline.

skill: High cervical injury / neurogenic versus haemorrhagic shock
stem: A 28-year-old falls from a ladder and has weakness in all four limbs. BP is 78/45 mmHg, pulse is 48/min and skin is warm and dry. A cervical injury is suspected, but he also has pelvic tenderness and possible intra-abdominal injury. The team is considering neurogenic shock as the sole cause of hypotension.
ask: Which immediate strategy best avoids a dangerous diagnostic assumption?
options: Treat bradycardia as proof that blood loss is absent and begin vasopressors alone.
Resuscitate as trauma, exclude haemorrhage and support perfusion while protecting the spine.
Administer high-dose methylprednisolone immediately to reverse cord swelling before imaging.
Place the patient upright to improve venous return and reassess pressure after mobilisation.
Delay vascular access until a complete formal spinal injury classification has been documented.
explanations: Bradycardia and warm skin suggest sympathetic disruption but cannot rule out concurrent haemorrhage. Assuming neurogenic shock alone risks missing a treatable fatal bleed.
Correct: follow major-trauma ABCDE and haemorrhage control with spinal precautions. After assessing blood loss, neurogenic hypotension may require titrated fluids and vasopressors.
High-dose steroids are not routinely recommended in acute spinal cord injury; benefits are uncertain and adverse effects can be substantial.
Upright positioning may worsen hypotension and risks moving an unstable spine. Controlled positioning and spinal protection are necessary.
Formal neurological classification helps later planning but must not delay airway, circulation, bleeding assessment or urgent transfer.
pearl: Bradycardia with hypotension suggests neurogenic shock, but traumatic haemorrhage must be excluded.
pivot: After bleeding is excluded, a high spinal injury with bradycardia and vasodilation supports neurogenic shock.

steps: Protect cervical alignment and address airway, breathing and circulation.
Assess pelvis, abdomen and chest using appropriate trauma imaging and examination.
Give titrated fluids and vasoactive support if neurogenic shock is likely.
Arrange urgent spinal specialist assessment while preventing hypoxia and hypotension.
management.safety: Do not attribute hypotension to neurogenic shock before assessing haemorrhage; avoid routine high-dose steroids.
management.local: Queensland Spinal Cord Injuries Service neurogenic shock guidance.

skill: Life-threatening haemoptysis / protecting unaffected lung
stem: A 56-year-old with bronchiectasis begins coughing large volumes of bright-red blood. He is hypoxic, confused and unable to clear his airway. A recent CT shows severe disease predominantly in the left lung, and current bleeding appears left-sided. BP is 105/65 mmHg after initial resuscitation.
ask: What should take priority before definitive embolisation or bronchoscopy?
options: Send the patient directly for CT angiography while keeping him flat to obtain clearer images.
Give a routine dose of tranexamic acid and defer airway planning until haemoglobin results return.
Protect oxygenation and position the suspected bleeding lung down with expert airway support.
Perform immediate diagnostic sputum culture because infection is the usual cause of haemoptysis.
Place the right lung dependent to drain blood away from the diseased left lower airways.
explanations: CT can guide embolisation once stable, but transporting a confused hypoxic patient with active airway flooding is unsafe without airway planning.
Antifibrinolytics may be adjuncts, but cannot replace suction, positioning and advanced airway care when asphyxiation is imminent.
Correct: preserve ventilation of the unaffected lung by placing the bleeding side down if known, suctioning and involving airway and respiratory specialists urgently.
Microbiology can be collected later and does not prevent immediate airway flooding. Life-threatening haemoptysis can kill by asphyxiation.
Placing the healthy right lung dependent encourages blood to spill into its airways. The suspected bleeding left lung should be down.
pearl: Protecting the unaffected lung is often more urgent than quantifying blood loss in massive haemoptysis.
pivot: Small-volume haemoptysis with preserved oxygenation can allow structured imaging and cause investigation.

steps: Call anaesthesia/ICU, give oxygen, suction and prepare definitive airway support.
Place the bleeding lung dependent when laterality is established.
Establish access, crossmatch blood and correct coagulopathy or shock.
Arrange bronchoscopy and bronchial artery embolisation or surgery as appropriate.
management.safety: Do not transfer an unstable patient to CT without airway planning or position the healthy lung dependent.
management.local: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation massive haemoptysis management aims.

skill: Smoke inhalation / impending upper-airway obstruction
stem: A 10-year-old is rescued from a house fire in an enclosed room. She has facial burns, soot in the mouth, a hoarse voice and increasing stridor. SpO2 reads 97% on room air, but her neck is swelling. The burn surface area appears relatively small and transfer to a burns centre will take two hours.
ask: Which decision is most important before transfer?
options: Defer airway intervention because pulse oximetry confirms sufficient oxygen carriage and adequate ventilation.
Treat the facial burn with topical dressing and reassess stridor after the transfer journey.
Use inhaled bronchodilators alone because airway swelling usually remains below the vocal cords.
Request expert early airway control and high-flow oxygen while arranging burns retrieval.
Offer oral fluids and observe because the visible skin burn percentage is too small for critical injury.
explanations: Pulse oximetry can be falsely reassuring in carbon monoxide exposure and cannot measure progressive upper-airway obstruction. Stridor and intraoral soot are major warning signs.
Wound care is secondary to airway protection. Swelling can progress during transport and make later intubation difficult or impossible.
Bronchodilators may help lower-airway bronchospasm but cannot reliably reverse thermal upper-airway oedema or prevent obstruction.
Correct: early expert airway assessment and likely controlled intubation are needed with worsening stridor, hoarseness and swelling. Give high-flow oxygen and coordinate retrieval.
Visible skin burn extent does not reliably predict inhalation injury. Oral fluids also risk aspiration when airway compromise is developing.
pearl: Soot, hoarseness and stridor after an enclosed-space fire require early airway planning despite normal SpO2.
pivot: A stable isolated superficial limb burn without smoke exposure or airway symptoms follows a routine burn first-aid pathway.

steps: Perform ABCDE and check stridor, soot, hoarseness, oral oedema and associated trauma.
Give high-flow oxygen and evaluate carbon monoxide or cyanide exposure.
Request experienced paediatric airway staff for early controlled intervention.
Coordinate burns-centre retrieval, fluids, temperature control and wound care.
management.safety: Normal pulse oximetry cannot exclude carbon monoxide poisoning or impending inhalation-related airway obstruction.
management.local: RCH Burns – acute management clinical practice guideline (2026).

skill: Contact lens-associated microbial keratitis / urgent referral
stem: A 24-year-old who sleeps in soft contact lenses presents with severe unilateral eye pain, photophobia and reduced vision. The eye is red and fluorescein examination shows a central corneal epithelial defect with an underlying white infiltrate. There is no recent blunt trauma and she is afebrile.
ask: Which immediate plan best prevents permanent visual loss?
options: Treat as uncomplicated conjunctivitis with routine chloramphenicol and review in five days.
Patch the eye tightly and continue contact lenses to protect the exposed corneal surface.
Start topical corticosteroids without antimicrobial cover to reduce stromal inflammation rapidly.
Prescribe lubricating drops only because a corneal defect should heal after lens removal.
Stop contact lenses and arrange same-day ophthalmology-led microbial keratitis treatment.
explanations: A central corneal ulcer with reduced vision is not simple conjunctivitis. Low-intensity therapy risks progression, particularly with contact-lens-associated Pseudomonas.
Patching may promote infection and delays inspection. Contact lenses should be stopped, not used as a dressing.
Steroids may worsen active infection without adequate antimicrobial cover. Any later role is an ophthalmologist-directed decision.
Lubrication alone cannot eradicate microbial keratitis. Central infiltration risks scarring, perforation and permanent visual loss.
Correct: remove lenses, document acuity, obtain same-day ophthalmology review and arrange corneal sampling and intensive topical antimicrobials as advised.
pearl: A painful photophobic red eye with reduced vision and corneal infiltrate in a lens wearer is keratitis until proven otherwise.
pivot: Bilateral itch and watery discharge with normal vision and no infiltrate suggests a different conjunctival pathway.

steps: Record visual acuity, pupil findings and fluorescein staining.
Remove lenses and avoid patching or unsupervised steroid drops.
Follow specialist antimicrobial, sampling and close-review instructions.
management.safety: Do not prescribe topical steroids or patch a suspected infected cornea without specialist direction.
management.local: Queensland Health ophthalmology emergency referral criteria for contact-lens keratitis.

skill: Dirty puncture wound / tetanus prophylaxis
stem: A 42-year-old gardener steps on a nail contaminated with soil. He has a puncture wound on his foot, but no systemic symptoms. He cannot recall any tetanus vaccinations and records are unavailable. The wound is being cleaned.
ask: Which prevention strategy is appropriate for this wound and vaccination history?
options: Give tetanus-containing vaccine and tetanus immunoglobulin as indicated after wound cleaning.
Give tetanus vaccine alone because passive antibodies are never needed in healthy adults.
Prescribe oral antibiotics instead of immunisation because soil contamination makes vaccination ineffective.
Give tetanus immunoglobulin alone because active immunisation has no value after the wound occurs.
Delay prophylaxis until a tetanus antibody titre is returned to avoid unnecessary treatment.
explanations: Correct: a contaminated puncture is tetanus-prone. Unknown or incomplete vaccination history warrants cleaning, active tetanus vaccination and passive tetanus immunoglobulin under the Australian Immunisation Handbook.
Vaccine creates long-term protection but does not supply immediate antitoxin in a potentially unimmunised person. TIG is indicated for qualifying wounds.
Antibiotics may address separate wound infection concerns but do not replace tetanus vaccination or immunoglobulin in tetanus-prone wounds.
TIG provides short-term protection only. A primary vaccine course is still needed to establish durable immunity.
Immediate prophylaxis depends on wound risk and vaccination history. Waiting for a titre is not routine and can delay protection.
pearl: Tetanus-prone wounds with unknown vaccination history may need both vaccine and TIG.
pivot: A fully vaccinated patient with a recent appropriate booster may need cleaning alone or a booster depending on timing.

steps: Irrigate, remove debris and assess foreign-body or deeper injury.
Review vaccine history if readily available without delaying care.
Give indicated vaccine and TIG at separate sites under handbook guidance.
Arrange completion of the vaccine course and wound review.
management.safety: TIG and vaccine are not interchangeable; both accompany adequate wound care when indicated.
management.local: Victorian Department of Health tetanus guidance and Australian Immunisation Handbook.

skill: Uncomplicated osteomyelitis / IV-to-oral transition
stem: A 6-year-old has MRI-confirmed uncomplicated acute haematogenous osteomyelitis of the tibia. Blood culture grows methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. After three days of IV cefazolin he is afebrile, walking comfortably, tolerating food and his CRP is falling. There is no abscess or joint involvement.
ask: Which next step best balances effective treatment and avoiding unnecessary IV exposure?
options: Continue six weeks of IV antibiotics regardless of response because all bone infections need prolonged access.
Consider oral step-down using a susceptible agent with planned follow-up and total course duration.
Stop all antibiotics immediately because three days of improvement proves eradication of bone infection.
Arrange operative debridement solely because the original MRI demonstrated marrow oedema.
Switch to topical antibiotics because bacterial growth is confined to the tibial cortex.
explanations: Complicated infections may require longer IV therapy, but uncomplicated improving cases can switch early. Mandatory six-week IV treatment is not current standard.
Correct: after about two to three days of IV treatment, clinical improvement and falling markers may support suitable oral therapy with follow-up.
Clinical response does not prove eradication after three days. Premature discontinuation increases relapse risk.
Surgery is for abscess, treatment failure or complications, not uncomplicated marrow oedema responding to antibiotics.
Topical medicines do not achieve therapeutic concentrations in infected bone. Systemic antibiotics remain necessary.
pearl: Uncomplicated paediatric osteomyelitis often permits early oral step-down after improvement.
pivot: Persistent fever, rising CRP, abscess or septic joint calls for specialist reassessment and possible surgery.

steps: Review organism, susceptibilities, imaging and absence of complications.
Document fever resolution, improving pain and falling CRP.
Choose oral therapy and total duration with paediatric advice.
Arrange clinical and laboratory review with return precautions.
management.safety: Do not switch to oral treatment with persistent sepsis, poor absorption or an uncontrolled focus.
management.local: RCH Bone and joint infection clinical practice guideline.

skill: Tension pneumothorax / immediate decompression
stem: A 36-year-old trauma patient is intubated after a motorbike collision. Immediately after positive-pressure ventilation starts, oxygen saturation falls to 76%, BP to 65/35 mmHg and right-sided breath sounds are absent. The trachea is difficult to assess, and the portable chest radiograph machine is several minutes away.
ask: Which immediate action best addresses the likely reversible cause?
options: Wait for a portable radiograph because unilateral breath sounds alone are insufficient for intervention.
Increase positive end-expiratory pressure to recruit the affected lung before further investigation.
Decompress the suspected tension pneumothorax immediately and arrange definitive chest drainage.
Give IV furosemide because pulmonary oedema is the most likely cause of shock in this setting.
Disconnect all monitoring and transfer directly to CT to confirm the cause of hypoxaemia.
explanations: Radiography may help stable diagnostic uncertainty, but shock with abrupt unilateral absent breath sounds after ventilation demands immediate action.
Higher airway pressure can worsen tension physiology and obstruct venous return. Ventilator checks should occur alongside urgent decompression.
Correct: suspected tension pneumothorax with shock warrants immediate trained needle or open thoracostomy, followed by definitive chest drainage and reassessment.
Diuresis does not relieve pleural pressure and may worsen hypotension. Pulmonary oedema is less consistent with abrupt unilateral findings.
CT transfer is dangerous in an unstable patient with a rapidly reversible obstructive cause. Stabilisation and decompression take priority.
pearl: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis in shock; decompress without waiting for radiography.
pivot: A stable small pneumothorax without compromise may follow observation or planned drainage according to context.

steps: Check tube position, circuit, unilateral breath sounds and obstructive shock signs.
Perform immediate trained pleural decompression on the affected side.
Insert definitive chest drainage and reassess ventilation and blood pressure.
Repeat trauma survey and imaging once stable; assess other shock causes.
management.safety: Do not increase positive pressure or delay decompression for imaging when tension physiology is suspected.
management.local: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10 Resuscitation in Special Circumstances (2026).

skill: Acute liver failure / early transplant centre referral
stem: A 27-year-old with no known chronic liver disease presents after several days of vomiting and malaise. ALT is 3800 U/L, INR 3.6, glucose 2.8 mmol/L and she is intermittently disoriented. Paracetamol exposure is uncertain and initial viral serology is pending. She has no history of cirrhosis or ascites.
ask: What is the safest next management priority?
options: Arrange outpatient repeat liver tests in two days because transaminases often fall spontaneously.
Treat with lactulose alone because altered mentation implies uncomplicated hepatic encephalopathy.
Wait for viral serology and paracetamol concentration before discussing definitive management.
Begin critical-care support and immediate liver-transplant centre discussion while investigating causes.
Give vitamin K and discharge if the INR improves because synthetic failure is then excluded.
explanations: Marked injury with coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia and encephalopathy is acute liver failure, not an outpatient monitoring problem.
Lactulose alone cannot address cerebral oedema risk, hypoglycaemia, synthetic dysfunction or transplant evaluation. Critical care is needed.
Cause-specific tests are important but may be delayed. Referral and consideration of N-acetylcysteine should occur in parallel.
Correct: stabilise glucose and organ function, contact ICU and a transplant-capable liver unit early, investigate aetiology and discuss empiric N-acetylcysteine.
Transient INR improvement after vitamin K does not make encephalopathy and hypoglycaemia safe. Discharge is inappropriate.
pearl: New coagulopathy and encephalopathy without cirrhosis indicate acute liver failure and early specialist referral.
pivot: Severe transaminitis with normal INR and mental status is acute liver injury but not necessarily liver failure.

steps: Assess ABCDE and treat hypoglycaemia immediately.
Contact ICU, hepatology and a transplant centre without waiting for tests.
Check paracetamol, viral/autoimmune causes, coagulation, renal function and lactate.
Discuss N-acetylcysteine, cause-specific treatment and cerebral oedema surveillance.
management.safety: Falling ALT or transient INR improvement does not establish recovery; follow synthetic function and mental status.
management.local: Queensland Health acute liver failure emergency referral criteria.

skill: Postpartum iron deficiency / IV iron versus transfusion
stem: A 29-year-old is five days postpartum after a delivery complicated by moderate blood loss. Haemoglobin is 82 g/L, ferritin is low and she reports fatigue and mild dizziness on standing. She is haemodynamically stable, bleeding has stopped, there is no chest pain or dyspnoea, and she cannot tolerate oral iron.
ask: Which treatment option is most appropriate after clinical assessment and shared decision-making?
options: Arrange immediate red-cell transfusion for every postpartum haemoglobin below 90 g/L.
Discharge without iron replacement because postpartum haemoglobin normally corrects itself.
Start oral iron despite intolerance and defer reassessment until the next pregnancy.
Give prophylactic antibiotics because postpartum anaemia is most commonly caused by infection.
Offer intravenous iron with monitoring and follow-up rather than automatic blood transfusion.
explanations: Transfusion may be needed with bleeding, severe symptoms or instability, but stable mild symptoms at Hb 82 g/L do not mandate red cells.
Postpartum iron deficiency impairs recovery and can persist without replacement. Observation alone does not address depleted iron stores.
Oral iron is often first-line, but this patient cannot tolerate it. Insisting on an unsuitable regimen risks prolonged fatigue.
Low ferritin after blood loss is not evidence of infection. Antibiotics do not restore iron and are inappropriate without infection.
Correct: stable mildly symptomatic postpartum patients with Hb 70–90 g/L may be offered IV iron instead of transfusion when oral treatment is unsuitable.
pearl: Stable postpartum iron deficiency with Hb 70–90 g/L can often be treated with IV iron rather than transfusion.
pivot: Ongoing bleeding, syncope, chest pain, marked dyspnoea or instability prompts urgent resuscitation and transfusion assessment.

steps: Review vital signs, ongoing bleeding, symptoms and anaemia causes.
Check FBC, ferritin and relevant iron studies.
Discuss IV iron formulation, risks and alternatives under maternity protocol.
Monitor administration and repeat haemoglobin and iron studies.
management.safety: IV iron is not a substitute for urgent blood support during active bleeding or severe instability.
management.local: Metro North Health IV iron therapy guideline, maternity appendix, April 2026.

skill: Congenital CMV / time-limited diagnostic sampling
stem: A 13-day-old infant fails the repeat newborn hearing screen on the left. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated, examination is normal and parents ask whether the hearing test can simply be repeated at three months. Congenital cytomegalovirus has not yet been assessed.
ask: Which investigation should be organised promptly to establish whether congenital CMV is present?
options: Collect saliva CMV PCR now and confirm a positive result with urine PCR within 21 days.
Request CMV IgG from the mother and defer infant sampling until the hearing review.
Arrange a routine infant CMV IgM assay at three months instead of early virology.
Use cranial ultrasound alone because a normal scan would exclude congenital CMV.
